4.3.2. The plaintiff does not allege any violations of the non-competition clause other than those 
found by the lower court. Nor does she present any arguments that would demonstrate that the 
lower court’s findings of fact were arbitrary. This is particularly the case when she asserts—
without substantiating this in any way—that the lower court erroneously assumed that she was 
not working for Construction21 at the time the expert’s letter was written. The lower court 
provided a convincing rationale for why it assumed that what was described was “virtually the 
same” as the “takeover of the operational business” (see E. 4.2.2 above). The plaintiff’s reference 
in this regard to an email sent to a candidate does not establish arbitrariness. The same applies to 
her argument that the lower court wrongly assumed she had failed to demonstrate the risk of 
damage. For example, in connection with the alleged confusion among experts (see above, para. 
4.2.5), the plaintiff merely conducts her own assessment of the evidence, while still failing to 
demonstrate that more than just one candidate was “confused.” In this respect, the appeal does 
not meet the requirements for a statement of grounds. It need not be addressed. 
4.3.3. The arguments raised by the parties regarding the amount of the contractual penalty based 
on the violations of the non-competition clause do not constitute a violation of federal law.  
It is undisputed that the defendant argued in the proceedings that the contractual penalty was 
“excessive” and should be reduced by the court. As explained, the plaintiff also fails to present 
any arguments that would demonstrate the lower court’s findings of fact—which formed the 
basis for assessing the reasonableness of the contractual penalty, specifically regarding the 
severity of the violation and the absence of damage—to be arbitrary. Contrary to the plaintiff’s 
view, it is therefore not objectionable—in light of the principle of party disposition—that the 
lower court reduced the contractual penalty at its discretion. It did not violate this principle 
either. 
Rather, the lower court reasonably concluded that there is a gross disproportion between the 
agreed amount of the contractual penalty and the plaintiff’s interest in receiving the full 
contractual penalty at the time of the breach. The plaintiff has not demonstrated otherwise. It is 
not sufficient to point out that the terms wrongfully used by the defendant are registered 
trademarks. The plaintiff has not substantiated why a penalty of CHF 50,000 to CHF 100,000 
would be appropriate solely for that reason. The same applies to the fact that a mutual non-
